btos.label: Real estate and rental and leasing (NAICS 53)

name: Real Estate

points.name: AVMs are now federally regulated AI

points.name: Smart buildings close the operations loop

summary: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest deployed AI, and it is now formally regulated: federal quality-control standards for AVMs took effect in 2025. Valuation, leasing automation, 3D capture, and property operations are where AI actually runs; the regulator record and the platforms' own model documentation are the sources.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 28.0% of firms in real estate and rental and leasing reported using AI in the most recent period, up from 25.6% in the prior period, making this one of the more measurable adoption signals available for the sector. The figure covers actual two-week use reported by firms rather than intent or pilot activity, so it reflects tools already running inside businesses rather than plans on a roadmap.

The oldest and most consequential AI in the sector is the automated valuation model, and it now carries formal federal oversight. The FHFA, CFPB, OCC, Federal Reserve Board, FDIC, and NCUA jointly finalized quality control standards requiring mortgage originators and secondary market issuers that rely on AVMs for collateral determinations to adopt policies ensuring high confidence in estimates, protection against data manipulation, avoidance of conflicts of interest, and random sample testing and reviews. Zillow publishes Zestimate valuations for more than 110 million homes using a neural network that draws on county records, tax assessor data, and MLS feeds, and the company states its latest model architecture has helped reduce overall error rates while maintaining broad coverage. HouseCanary offers AI-powered valuations and analytics covering more than 136 million U.S. properties, combining machine learning with image recognition that assesses home condition directly from photos. Opendoor takes the AVM a step further by using pricing models to make direct purchase offers to homeowners, placing real balance-sheet exposure behind the model's output.

On the commercial side, the deployment picture spans portfolio analytics, lease administration, and building operations. JLL states it has invested more in AI technology than any other real estate company, applying it across brokerage, facilities, and portfolio analytics. Prophia uses AI to extract key lease terms from commercial lease documents and combines that extraction with expert validation to produce structured data that owners and operators can use for risk identification and capital protection. Building Engines, a JLL company, markets its Prism platform as an AI-powered system for running commercial property operations end to end, with the stated goals of cutting costs and growing net operating income. Matterport digitizes physical buildings into 3D models and integrates with Procore and Autodesk, positioning the captured spatial data as a layer for portfolio management, workplace planning, and remote operations.

Leasing and tenant communication represent a distinct automation front. EliseAI describes itself as an agentic AI platform that handles inbound messages, phone calls, tour scheduling, prospect follow-up, and maintenance requests around the clock, integrating with existing property management systems to deliver responses without staff involvement. The company positions this as a way to reduce overhead and free staff for higher-value work, though the sources do not report specific measured savings figures. Compass, on the residential brokerage side, embeds AI in agent workflows and offers a Concierge program that funds pre-sale home improvements, with the cost deferred until closing, as part of a broader platform approach to the transaction. CREtech convenes what it describes as the world's premier real estate AI conference, drawing 3,000 leaders and facilitating more than 20,000 pre-scheduled meetings, which itself signals how much strategic attention commercial real estate is paying to AI deployment.

The regulatory picture is clearer for AVMs than for any other AI application in the sector, and that clarity carries compliance obligations that buyers of valuation technology must account for. The interagency rule requires institutions to put written policies in place, conduct random sample testing, and document how conflicts of interest are managed, meaning the days of deploying an AVM in a lending context without formal governance are over. The CFPB's parallel work on algorithmic appraisal adds a consumer protection lens focused on valuation bias and model accountability. Outside the AVM context, the sector's AI governance is less settled, and the National Association of Realtors and BOMA International both serve as channels through which agents, brokers, and commercial building managers receive guidance on emerging tools and industry standards. For a decision-maker weighing deployment, the practical takeaway is that valuation AI touching mortgage decisions now requires a compliance program, leasing and operations automation is shipping in production at scale with vendors like EliseAI and Building Engines, and the proptech investment community tracked by CRETI and the NAR REACH accelerator continues to vet and fund the next generation of tools across both residential and commercial segments.
